Data Science Pipeline DSL 
ii 
Abstract 
Data science pipeline descriptions contain dependencies that can be checked before an 
execution engine is invoked. This project implements a domain -specific language and 
compiler front -end for expressing such descriptions as one named pipeline. The language 
supports dataset declarations, cleaning, column selection and dropping, percentage -based 
partitions, model declarations and evaluation requests. A regular -expression lexer produces 
tokens with source coordinates. A hand -written recursive -descent parser c onstructs a 
dataclass-based abstract syntax tree. Semantic analysis traverses the tree with a symbol table 
to enforce declaration, ordering, column and partition constraints. A lowering stage produces 
opcode-and-argument instructions. Four optimizer passes remove instructions after the final 
evaluation, eliminate unused training declarations, merge adjacent drops and collapse 
adjacent duplicate cleaning or selection instructions. A symbolic executor formats the 
optimized instructions as a readable trace; no  dataset contents are read and no numerical 
model training or accuracy calculation is performed. A command -line interface exposes 
intermediate results, while a Streamlit dashboard presents the same compiler stages 
interactively. Validation records 267 passing tests and the outcomes of all 20 supplied 
example programs. Optimizer tests compare symbolic evaluation records, test transformation 
boundaries and check repeated optimization. Recorded benchmark measurements are 
examined by stage, time per statement a nd instruction reduction. The results demonstrate an 
inspectable compiler pipeline within a deliberately restricted language, with explicit limits on 
execution, schema validation and error recovery.

Chapter 1 Introduction 
1.1 Background and problem area 
A pipeline describes an ordered set of operations whose later steps depend on earlier 
declarations. Even a short workflow introduces relationships between a dataset, selected 
columns, named partitions and models. A textual description becomes easier to inspect when 
these relationships are represented as language rules rather than scattered across execution 
code. 
Compiler construction provides a suitable separation of concerns. Lexical analysis recognizes 
the vocabulary, parsing establishes grammatical structure, and semantic analysis checks 
contextual relationships. A valid representation can then be lowered and transformed before 
an interpreter or another back end consumes it [1]. This project applies those stages to a 
restricted data science pipeline language. 
1.2 Motivation 
An ordering mistake such as training before defining a training partition can be identified 
without opening a dataset. Similarly, duplicate model names and percentages outside the 
accepted range are properties of the program description. Detecting these cases before a 
concrete runtime is invoked makes the source of a failure easier to isolate. 
The project therefore concentrates on inspectable language processing. It does not measure 
time saved by avoiding real training jobs. The executor is deliberately symbolic, making 
demonstrations independent of dataset availability and machine learning libraries. The 
resulting traces expose instruction order without implying numerical computation. 
1.3 Language and implementation overview 
A source file contains one pipeline declaration. Its body may contain load, clean, select, 
drop, split, train and evaluate statements. The root declaration names the program; it is not 
an eighth executable body operation. The parser accepts an empty body, and semantics does 
not impose a final mandatory-load check on such a body. 
The compiler package is ds_pipeline_dsl. It is driven by a command -line interface and 
reused by a Streamlit dashboard. Both expose actual compiler results. The dashboard adds 
presentation, stage timing and partial -result display without introducing new language 
statements. 
1.4 Report organization 
Chapters 2-4 establish the problem, objectives and background. Chapters 5 -8 explain design, 
development, compiler concepts and implementation. Chapter 9 evaluates the results, 
followed by conclusions and future work. Appendices provide the grammar, diagnostics, 
listings, examples, reproduction commands and phase evolution.

Chapter 2 Problem Statement 
2.1 Problem definition 
The problem is to design and implement a small language processor that accepts a pipeline 
description, rejects malformed or contextually inconsistent programs with source -referenced 
diagnostics, and translates accepted programs into an inspectable instruction sequence. The 
processor must keep recognition, structural analysis, state validation and execution 
presentation separate. 
Validation performed only after a concrete workflow begins can discover description errors 
later than necessary. This project demonstrates earlier detection for the specific invariants 
encoded in its semantic analyzer. It does not establish that general -purpose tools lack 
validation, nor does it provide a universal static analyzer for arbitrary Python programs.

3.2 Scope decisions and additional outcomes 
Semantic dependency checking and argument constraints are implemented, including 
percentage bounds, duplicate names and selected/dropped -column relationships. Multiple 
pipeline scopes, a general type system and allowed-value lists for strategy or algorithm names 
were not pursued. Names such as a custom cleaning strategy remain valid identifiers. This 
limitation makes the semantic -analysis objective partial rather than implying implementation 
of a full type checker. 
The final language adds drop beyond the Phase 1 grammar. The optimizer expands to four 
explicit passes, and the project includes a benchmark and dashboard. These additions extend 
the demonstration while retaining symbolic execution. ANTLR4 was considered in the 
proposal but was not adopted; lexical analysis and parsing remain hand-written.

Chapter 4 Literature Survey or Background Study 
4.1 Workflow orchestration and library pipelines 
Apache Airflow represents workflows as DAGs of tasks with dependencies and a 
scheduler/executor architecture [7]. Luigi supports dependency resolution and management 
of batch-task workflows [8]. Their task -level execution concerns are broader than the small 
source language implemented here. These systems should not be described as having no 
validation; this project instead makes its own statement-level semantic rules explicit. 
Kubeflow Pipelines provides a platform for machine learning workflows [9]. Its pipeline 
tooling is distinct from this project, which neither deploys containers nor executes machine 
learning workloads. Scikit -learn Pipeline composes transformers and an optional final 
predictor through estimator interfaces [10]. It provides execution -oriented composition rather 
than the specific .pipe grammar, AST and source diagnostics implemented by this project.

4.2 Compiler foundations 
Lexical analysis groups characters into tokens using patterns. The Python re module supplies 
the compiled matching operations used by the scanner [3]. A parser then recognizes 
sequences of token types. Recursive descent is a top -down approach in which procedures 
follow grammar structure; it is suitable when the next token selects the required alternative 
without backtracking [2]. 
An AST stores semantic structure with less punctuation detail than the source. Dataclasses 
provide generated initialization and representation methods for the AST and IR objects [4]. A

symbol table records contextual information during a traversal. In this language it stores 
pipeline artifacts and definition lines rather than nested variable scopes. 
An intermediate representation separates source structure from transformations and 
execution. The representation here is a linear list of opcode/argument records, not a register -
based target language or a conventional three -address expression form. Optimization 
correctness is stated relative to the symbolic evaluation -record oracle implemented in the 
tests, rather than equality of every textual trace line. 
4.3 Gap addressed 
The project addresses the need for a small, inspectable example of compiler integration in a 
data science vocabulary. It exposes every representation, makes its invariants testable and 
produces deterministic traces for accepted examples. Its contribution is the combination of a 
restricted grammar, contextual validation, an explicit IR and checked transformations. It is 
not presented as a replacement for the execution platforms reviewed above.

5.4 Symbol table and IR design 
The symbol table models the state accumulated from earlier accepted statements. Definition -
line maps make duplicate diagnostics explain both the current and previous declaration. 
selected_columns=None is meaningful: a drop before any selection is permitted after load, 
whereas a drop after selection must be drawn from the current selection and must leave at 
least one selected column. The complete field list appears in Table 7.3. 
IRInstruction contains op: str  and args: dict . Every recognized statement is lowered to 
one instruction in source order. Source lines are stored in the argument dictionary so the 
optimizer can explain removed or merged operations. The pipeline root itself has no 
executable opcode.

6.3 Design decisions 
Hand-written regular-expression scanning and recursive -descent parsing keep the grammar -
to-code relationship explicit. The body alternatives begin with distinct keyword tokens, and 
optional list repetition is selected by commas. A generated parser was unnecessary for this 
grammar, so the proposed ANTLR4 alternative was not pursued. 
One pipeline per file avoids scope resolution across separate programs. Strategy and 
algorithm names remain free identifiers to avoid coupling syntax to a particular ML library.

First-error reporting limits cascading diagnostics, while the symbolic executor keeps the 
demonstration independent of data and training dependencies. Each choice reduces the 
implementation boundary in a way that can be explained and tested. 
6.4 Optimizer corrections and regression validation 
The Phase 2 optimizer captured in commit ab9fe03 sets a flag after encountering an 
OP_EVAL and removes every subsequent instruction. This is unsafe for a legal sequence 
containing a second model and evaluation. The final optimizer searches for the last evaluation 
before trimming the tail. Current regression and sensitivity tests make the lost -second-
evaluation case explicit. 
The earlier duplicate comparison includes all instruction arguments. Since lowering includes 
the source line in those arguments, identical operations on different lines can compare 
unequal. The final duplicate pass excludes line metadata from the semantic comparison while 
retaining it in surviving instructions and notes. 
Current tests exercise the corrected behaviors, compare each pass with an evaluation -record 
oracle and test repeated optimization. The available commit order does not establish whether 
tests were written before each implementation edit; the methodology is therefore described as 
regression-driven validation rather than an unsupported claim about test-first chronology. 
6.5 Reconciliation of earlier descriptions 
The final Token is a dataclass, despite the Phase 2 text referring to a namedtuple. The 
processor has dependency/state checks rather than general type inference or multiple -pipeline 
scope checking. An empty pipeline is accepted, so a mandatory single -load claim would be 
incorrect. Unused and trailing models may appear in the semantic symbol table because that 
table describes the original AST; optimization subsequently removes their IR instructions 
where permitted.

Chapter 7 Compiler Design Concepts Used 
7.1 Lexical analysis 
The scanner compiles the ordered TOKEN_SPEC alternatives into one master regular 
expression with named groups. finditer yields matches from left to right. Identifiers that 
exactly match a reserved word are converted to the corresponding uppercase keyword token. 
Keyword recognition therefore does not split a longer identifier such as trainer into a 
keyword and suffix. 
Table 7.1 preserves the actual regular expressions and their priority order. STRING precedes 
BAD_STRING, so a closed literal is recognized before the unterminated -string case. 
PERCENT precedes NUMBER, allowing the percentage suffix to form one token. EOF is 
appended explicitly and is not a regex alternative. 
Table 7.1 summarizes lexical patterns in scanner priority order. 
Table 7.1: Lexical patterns in scanner priority order

2 BAD_STRING "[^"\n]* Unterminated string detector 
3 PERCENT \d+(\.\d+)?% Numeric percentage with suffix 
4 NUMBER \d+(\.\d+)? Bare numeric literal 
5 LBRACE \{ Opening brace

The reserved words are clean, drop, evaluate, load, pipeline, select, split, train. 
Whitespace includes spaces, tabs, CR and LF. Line tracking counts LF characters; a CRLF 
sequence therefore advances one line. Comment text is ignored until LF. The identifier regex

is ASCII -based, while comments and strings can contain Unicode characters. The digit 
patterns use Python regular-expression \d, not a separately enforced ASCII digit alphabet. 
The scanner initializes line numbering to one and calculates columns as offsets from the 
current line start, making columns zero-based. The appended EOF token uses the current line 
and column zero. Unterminated strings and unexpected characters raise LexicalError. These 
are lexer errors rather than parser guesses about an invalid token. 
7.2 Syntax analysis 
pipeline_decl    ::= 'pipeline' IDENT '{' statement* '}' 
statement        ::= load_stmt 
                   | clean_stmt 
                   | select_stmt 
                   | drop_stmt 
                   | split_stmt 
                   | train_stmt 
                   | evaluate_stmt 
 
load_stmt        ::= 'load' STRING ';' 
clean_stmt       ::= 'clean' IDENT ';' 
select_stmt      ::= 'select' IDENT (',' IDENT)* ';' 
drop_stmt        ::= 'drop' IDENT (',' IDENT)* ';' 
split_stmt       ::= 'split' split_name '=' PERCENT ';' 
split_name       ::= IDENT | 'train' 
train_stmt       ::= 'train' IDENT '=' IDENT ';' 
evaluate_stmt    ::= 'evaluate' IDENT ';' 
The grammar above is taken from the parser specification and checked against its statement 
branches. parse_pipeline requires PIPELINE, an identifier and an opening brace; it 
repeatedly parses statements until a closing brace is found. It then requires the remaining 
token to be EOF, with a specific diagnostic for a second pipeline declaration. 
The body alternatives have pairwise -disjoint FIRST sets: LOAD, CLEAN, SELECT, DROP, 
SPLIT, TRAIN and EVALUATE. The repeated statement sequence stops on RBRACE. A 
column-list continuation is selected by COMMA and otherwise the parser expects SEMI. 
These choices require only one lookahead token and no backtracking. There is no left -
recursive production. This is the relevant LL(1) justification for the implemented grammar, 
rather than a claim about arbitrary grammar extensions. 
The split -name position accepts IDENT or TRAIN. The word test is already an ordinary 
identifier, so it needs no separate reserved -token alternative. Other reserved words are not 
accepted where a normal identifier is expected. Percentages are tokenized with the suffix 
present; a bare NUMBER at a split value leads to an expected-PERCENT syntax diagnostic. 
The parser uses peek, advance and expect to manage its token position. expect reports the 
required token type and the type/value found at the current token. A missing semicolon is 
often detected at the following statement token, so its error line can be later than the line 
where the omission occurred. This behavior is demonstrated by the supplied syntax -error 
example in Chapter 9.

7.4 Symbol table and semantic analysis 
Table 7.3 lists all instance fields initialized by SymbolTable. They are populated by a left -to-
right AST traversal. 
Table 7.3: SymbolTable fields 
Field Stored form Purpose

data_cleaned bool Whether at least one clean declaration has been accepted.

The analyzer creates a fresh table for each pipeline. A successful load sets the dataset flag 
and declaration line. Clean updates its flag. Select replaces the active selection with a copied 
list. Drop remembers removed names and, when a selection exists, filters those names out of 
the active selection. Split inserts its name and percentage. Train records the model and 
algorithm; evaluate checks that the model has already been recorded. 
The first training declaration also sets first_train. Clean, select and drop consult that field 
and are rejected after any model has been trained. A split after training remains legal if its 
own load, uniqueness and percentage conditions pass. Multiple evaluations are legal, 
including repeated evaluation of the same existing model. The analyzer does not require 
cleaning, selection, a test split or a final evaluation.

7.6 Four-pass optimization 
The optimizer calls _remove_unreachable, _remove_dead_trains, _merge_adjacent_drops 
and _collapse_duplicates in that order. Its notes parameter is optional. With a supplied list, 
transformations append diagnostic strings; with notes=None, no diagnostic print is required. 
Surviving instructions receive new record objects and copied argument dictionaries. Nested 
values such as column lists are not a general deep -copy guarantee, although the existing 
transformations do not mutate those input lists. 
7.6.1 Removal after the last evaluation 
Pass 1 searches backward for the final OP_EVAL and keeps instructions through that 
position. Instructions in the remaining tail cannot influence a later evaluation because no later

7.6.5 Observable behavior and safety limits 
The tests define an evaluation record as the tuple (model_name, algorithm, train_state, 
eval_state). A state snapshot contains cleaning history, selected columns, the dropped-column 
set and sorted split entries. Training stores its state snapshot; evaluation records both that 
stored state and current state. The comparison is therefore stronger than merely checking the 
final evaluation message. 
All preparation statements precede the first train in semantically accepted source. Removing 
an unused train therefore cannot bring previously separated preparation operations together. 
Splits can occur after training, so their timing remains significant: the oracle records the state 
at training separately from the state at evaluation. Only the tail after the last evaluation is 
discarded. 
Complete instruction traces need not be identical after optimization. A merged drop has 
different text and a removed train no longer has a trace line. Evaluation -record equality is the 
correctness target. Tests additionally check operation order, surviving evaluations, dropped -
column coverage, input preservation and idempotence on the supplied equivalence programs. 
If no evaluation exists, only the two removal passes are conservative. Adjacent -drop merging 
and duplicate collapse still run. The live no -evaluation specimen in the evidence reduces 
three instructions to two by collapsing a duplicate clean. Consequently, a blanket statement 
that optimize always leaves no-evaluation pipelines unchanged would be false.

def optimize(ir_list: List[IRInstruction], notes: Optional[list] = None) -> 
List[IRInstruction]: 
    """Optimizes the IR instructions through four independent passes: 
    1. _remove_unreachable: removes dead tail instructions after the final evaluation. 
    2. _remove_dead_trains: removes training of models that are never evaluated. 
    3. _merge_adjacent_drops: combines runs of adjacent drop instructions. 
    4. _collapse_duplicates: eliminates consecutive duplicate clean and select 
instructions. 
 
    Note on order: Order of passes is chosen for readability; the passes are independent 
    because all data-preparation statements precede the first train (F1). 
    """ 
    ir = _remove_unreachable(ir_list, notes) 
    ir = _remove_dead_trains(ir, notes) 
    ir = _merge_adjacent_drops(ir, notes) 
    ir = _collapse_duplicates(ir, notes) 
    return ir

8.6 Benchmark implementation 
The benchmark builds synthetic programs with repeated cleans, adjacent drops, repeated 
selects, evaluated and unevaluated model declarations, and one trailing training instruction. 
Its size parameter is not the final statement count. expected_counts derives the generated 
count, and correctness checks verify statement, IR and evaluation counts before timing. 
The driver performs an untimed warm -up, collects garbage between repetitions, disables 
garbage collection inside timed regions and uses inner loops to reduce timer quantization 
effects. Three repetitions are configured, with per -stage medians reported. Total ms is the 
sum of the lexer, parser, semantic, IR, optimizer and optimized -execution medians; 
unoptimized execution is measured separately. 
The safeguards bound the size parameter at 20000 and source length at 2000000 characters. 
A quadratic projection is checked against a 120 -second overall budget. A repetition longer 
than 30 seconds can reduce repetitions after it completes; this is a post -run check, not a 
preemptive timeout that interrupts a hanging call. These limits are reported as implemented 
rather than described as stronger runtime guarantees.

Chapter 10 Conclusion 
10.1 Achievements against objectives 
The completed system implements a restricted pipeline language through lexical analysis, 
predictive parsing, AST construction, symbol -table-based semantic checking, IR generation, 
four-pass optimization and symbolic execution. The CLI exposes intermediate 
representations and the dashboard makes the same processing stages accessible for interactive 
inspection. 
The verified run records 267 passing tests and outcomes for 20 supplied examples. The 
optimizer demonstration produces eleven original instructions and seven optimized 
instructions while preserving its evaluation records. The recorded performance table provides 
stage timings and instruction counts for the generated workloads. These results meet the core 
language-processing and demonstration objectives. 
10.2 Limitations 
Execution is symbolic only. A filename declaration does not prove that a dataset exists or that 
named columns occur in a schema. Cleaning strategies and training algorithms are free 
identifiers. The implementation has no general static type system, no allowed-value catalogue 
and no concrete estimator backend. 
Each source file contains one pipeline, and the compiler stops at its first expected error. It has 
no multi-error recovery, warning severity system, loops or user -defined functions. An empty 
pipeline is accepted. Optimizer safety is stated under the project test oracle and its symbolic 
preparation assumptions, not as a claim about arbitrary real data transformations. 
The benchmark scope is limited to the recorded machine and synthetic template. A passing 
test suite does not establish exhaustive input coverage. These boundaries distinguish the 
achieved compiler demonstration from the future extensions listed in Chapter 11. 
10.3 Learning outcomes 
The implementation connects grammar design with parser control flow, declaration rules with 
state management, and transformations with explicit observable behavior. The optimizer 
evolution demonstrates why source metadata must be separated from semantic equality and 
why later evaluations cannot be discarded simply because an earlier evaluation exists. 
Exposing intermediate results makes those decisions inspectable during a technical review.

Chapter 11 Future Enhancements 
11.1 Language and validation extensions 
An optional schema could restrict cleaning strategies and model algorithms and describe 
required arguments. Such a change would require an explicit language -policy decision, new 
diagnostics and tests; it should not be implied by the current identifier grammar. Dataset -
schema validation could be added separately with a clear distinction between source 
validation and external file inspection. 
Multiple pipeline declarations would require a new program root, pipeline symbol scopes and 
rules for cross-pipeline references. Statement-level recovery could synchronize at semicolons 
or closing braces and collect more diagnostics, while avoiding updates from invalid 
declarations. A separate warning channel could expose unused models or redundant 
preparation without treating them as fatal errors. 
11.2 Execution and optimization extensions 
A scale statement is a plausible language extension, but it would need coordinated lexer, 
AST, parser, semantic, IR, executor and test changes. Its transformation properties would 
need to be defined before any optimizer could remove or reorder it. 
A concrete execution backend could consume the existing IR through a separate runtime 
interface. It would need explicit dataset access, estimator dependencies, data partition 
semantics and error handling. The present symbolic idempotence assumptions would have to 
be reviewed for real algorithms, and equivalence tests would need observable results 
appropriate to that backend. 
11.3 Evaluation extensions 
Further evaluation could use additional program families, varied numbers of splits and 
columns, memory profiling, and multiple runtime environments. Property -based generation 
could complement the present example and boundary tests. Dashboard validation could add a 
supported browser -rendering check. These are prospective enhancements, not features or 
measurements claimed for the completed implementation.

Appendix A Final Grammar and Lexical Specification 
A.1 Final EBNF 
The grammar is copied from parser.py. After the closing brace, the parser checks for EOF 
and rejects trailing input. TRAIN is contextual in split_name; test remains IDENT. 
pipeline_decl    ::= 'pipeline' IDENT '{' statement* '}' 
statement        ::= load_stmt 
                   | clean_stmt 
                   | select_stmt 
                   | drop_stmt 
                   | split_stmt 
                   | train_stmt 
                   | evaluate_stmt 
 
load_stmt        ::= 'load' STRING ';' 
clean_stmt       ::= 'clean' IDENT ';' 
select_stmt      ::= 'select' IDENT (',' IDENT)* ';' 
drop_stmt        ::= 'drop' IDENT (',' IDENT)* ';' 
split_stmt       ::= 'split' split_name '=' PERCENT ';' 
split_name       ::= IDENT | 'train' 
train_stmt       ::= 'train' IDENT '=' IDENT ';' 
evaluate_stmt    ::= 'evaluate' IDENT ';' 
A.2 Lexical details 
Table 7.1 gives regex priority. Keywords are case -sensitive; lines are one-based and columns 
zero-based. Whitespace accepts CRLF and LF. Comments extend from // to LF or EOF. 
Double-quoted strings exclude LF and have no escape-sequence decoding.

from dataclasses import dataclass 
from typing import List 
from ds_pipeline_dsl.ast_nodes import ( 
    PipelineNode, LoadStmt, CleanStmt, SelectStmt, DropStmt, 
    SplitStmt, TrainStmt, EvaluateStmt 
) 
from ds_pipeline_dsl.semantic import SymbolTable 
 
@dataclass 
class IRInstruction: 
    op: str 
    args: dict 
 
def lower_to_ir(pipeline_ast: PipelineNode, symbol_table: SymbolTable) -> 
List[IRInstruction]: 
    ir = [] 
    for stmt in pipeline_ast.statements: 
        if isinstance(stmt, LoadStmt): 
            ir.append(IRInstruction(op="OP_LOAD", args={"filename": stmt.filename, 
"line": stmt.line})) 
        elif isinstance(stmt, CleanStmt): 
            ir.append(IRInstruction(op="OP_CLEAN", args={"strategy": stmt.strategy, 
"line": stmt.line})) 
        elif isinstance(stmt, SelectStmt): 
            ir.append(IRInstruction(op="OP_SELECT", args={"columns": stmt.columns, 
"line": stmt.line})) 
        elif isinstance(stmt, DropStmt): 
            ir.append(IRInstruction(op="OP_DROP", args={"columns": stmt.columns, "line": 
stmt.line})) 
        elif isinstance(stmt, SplitStmt): 
            ir.append(IRInstruction(op="OP_SPLIT", args={"name": stmt.name, "percent": 
stmt.percent, "line": stmt.line})) 
        elif isinstance(stmt, TrainStmt): 
            ir.append(IRInstruction(op="OP_TRAIN", args={"model_name": stmt.model_name, 
"algorithm": stmt.algorithm, "line": stmt.line})) 
        elif isinstance(stmt, EvaluateStmt): 
            ir.append(IRInstruction(op="OP_EVAL", args={"model_name": stmt.model_name, 
"line": stmt.line})) 
    return ir

        elif instr.op == "OP_DROP": 
            cols = ", ".join(instr.args["columns"])

            percent = instr.args["percent"] 
            if percent == int(percent):

            trace.append(f"Defined split '{instr.args['name']}' = {percent}%")

            trace.append(f"Evaluated model '{instr.args['model_name']}' (simulated
